- WRD-1: noun items such as Status bar and Full screen without a verb appear in Kvit-drawn menus on Linux.
- WRD-4: Settings, Options and Properties carry no ellipsis on Linux.
- WRD-6: sentence case for buttons, menus and tabs; KDE apps use title case and GNOME header capitalisation for these, so Kvit will differ from neighbouring Linux apps.
- WRD-7: OK on settings windows, Yes/No on yes-or-no questions and a lone Close on information messages appear on Linux.
- WRD-8: Cancel turns into Close or Stop, and may be replaced by a specific negative answer, on Linux.
- WRD-12: Kvit-drawn menus on Linux keep a toggle's name and show a tick; the tray menu (StatusNotifierItem, dbusmenu) needs a checkable item.
- WRD-13: tooltips carry the shortcut in parentheses (Bold (Ctrl+B)) on Linux.
- WRD-17: help text says click for menu items on Linux.
- WRD-19: field labels end with a colon and prompts disappear on focus on Linux.
- WRD-20: group labels above controls end with a colon; menu titles may be verbs.
- WRD-21: flows end with Close, never Done, on Linux, though GNOME apps use Done.
- WRD-23: help says 'notification area'; on Linux desktops the place is called the system tray or status area, so help text naming it needs a Linux wording or none.
- WRD-24: Ctrl+Shift+N form and Enter/Page Up names on Linux; the logo key is called Super there (unison prints Super+).
- CTL-2: up to seven radio buttons before a select, and radio buttons on guided-flow pages.
- CTL-5: a mixed checkbox cycles back to the original mix; dependent labels end with a colon and share an access key.
- CTL-8: commit buttons stay enabled unless the reason is obvious, where GNOME apps often disable them.
- CTL-9: stepper takes Up and Down keys and wraps; slider paired with a field only when both are needed.
- CTL-10: up to seven tabs in a row, a vertical tab list from eight.
- CTL-11: no column browser; a tree for hierarchies deeper than two levels.
- CTL-15: window search at the top trailing corner, or centred when it is the entry point.
- CTL-16: disclosures read More options / Fewer options and Show details / Hide details.
- CTL-25: command links, which GNOME does not have, are Kvit-drawn on Linux.
- LAY-3: the 800 × 600 floor matters on small Linux laptops and scaled displays.
- LAY-6: field labels before the field on its baseline or above it.
- LAY-7: a dialog about one object opens beside it, offset down and right.
- MSG-1: a background dialog asks for attention through the urgency hint (X11) or xdg-activation (Wayland), the counterparts of flashing the taskbar button.
- MSG-6: GNOME and KDE show field problems inline as Kvit does; the Windows balloon form would look foreign there.
- MSG-10: freedesktop notifications commonly carry background failures, so the Windows form (an ignorable failure may notify) fits Linux too.
- MSG-11: freedesktop servers impose no 63/255 limits; the Windows lengths are kept so strings and translations are the same on both.
- MSG-13: freedesktop notifications support action buttons, but the Windows form (no buttons, click opens a window) is used; the backend's default action is labelled Open (`platform/tray_linux.go:386`).
- MSG-17: GNOME shows no StatusNotifierItem without an extension, so status that lives only on the tray icon can be invisible; Tray.Available reports it.
- FDB-2: the busy pointer uses the cursor theme's watch and progress cursors.
- FDB-3: Cancel versus Stop wording applies on Linux as on Windows.
- KEY-2: Redo is Ctrl+Y in the Windows form while Linux desktops use Ctrl+Shift+Z (open question); F1, F2, F5, Alt+F4 apply on Linux too.
- KEY-3: Ctrl+Alt combinations are also taken by Linux desktops (workspaces, terminals), and AltGr typing applies, so the ban matters there.
- KEY-4: the Super key plays the Windows logo key's part on GNOME and KDE and is reserved the same way.
- KEY-5: Ctrl+Q is free in the Windows list but quits apps on Linux desktops.
- KEY-6: Enter pressing the focused button and a default in every dialog match GTK and Qt dialogs.
- KEY-9: Ctrl+Tab and Ctrl+Page Up/Down switch tabs in GTK and Qt as on Windows.
- KEY-10: every interactive control a Tab stop, which GTK and Qt also do.
- KEY-11: Ctrl+wheel zoom and the wheel-button click (which pastes the primary selection in Linux text fields, so autoscroll must not take it there).
- KEY-12: Alt+drag moves windows in many Linux window managers, so keeping Alt off pointer gestures matters doubly.
- KEY-13: Ctrl+E is not a Linux convention; Ctrl+F is (open question).
- KEY-15: GTK and Qt use Alt mnemonics as Windows does; dbusmenu marks them with an underscore (`platform/tray_linux.go:445`).
- PTR-1: StatusNotifierItem hosts differ in what a left click does; some open the menu on any click, so the default command must also be in the menu.
- PTR-15: Ctrl-click toggles, as on Windows.
- A11Y-4: Linux desktops offer 125 and 150 percent fractional scaling too, so the scale test applies.
- CMD-1: Windows' menu bar in the window, with its hide-and-Alt route, where GNOME apps use a header-bar menu instead.
- CMD-2: File, Edit, View, Tools, Help on Linux, with Options in Tools, where GNOME and KDE apps differ among themselves.
- CMD-3: About in Help and Options in Tools rather than GNOME's primary menu with Preferences and About.
- CMD-10: the default item marked bold and the standard items kept disabled in Kvit-drawn context menus.
- CMD-11: shortcuts shown in context menus on Linux.
- CMD-12: no submenus in Linux context menus.
- CMD-15: bullet for exclusive options, which also matches GTK and Qt.
- CMD-16: no modifier-revealed alternates in Kvit-drawn menus on Linux.
- CMD-24: the tray menu and its order on Linux (StatusNotifierItem); GNOME shows tray icons only with an extension, so nothing may live only in the tray.
- WIN-1: the confirming button first (left); GNOME puts it last as macOS does, KDE as Windows does.
- WIN-6: the close control on every dialog and dialogs titled with the command that opened them.
- WIN-7: helper dialogs stacked over their owner.
- WIN-11: maximise and restore rather than a separate full-screen mode, and the 800×600 floor.
- WIN-12: "document - program" window titles.
- WIN-15: F11 and Esc for full screen, the usual keys on Linux desktops too.
- WIN-16: Options with OK and Cancel where GNOME apps use a live Preferences window.
- WIN-19: Save, Don't save, Cancel when closing with unsaved changes.
- WIN-23: OK/Cancel/Apply commit semantics in settings windows.
- WIN-25: placement and taskbar flashing; on Wayland the compositor may ignore an app's placement and focus requests, so the rule is best effort there.
- HLP-6: GNOME and KDE dialogs use a Help button; the Windows form puts a question-worded link at the bottom of the content instead, so Kvit apps on Linux differ from native Linux dialogs.
- HLP-2: the Windows infotip (a longer hover description for files and list items) applies on Linux too; GNOME has no such convention, so it must stay supplemental.
- CON-5: Linux desktops expose no hover-time or message-duration setting the way Windows does, so on Linux the tooltip timing keeps fixed defaults; platform.HoverTime must report "none" there.
- HLP-8: help on Linux uses the Windows terms (access keys, context menu, menu bar), which match KDE and GNOME usage closely enough.
